name: Second Battle of Panipat
info: On 5 November 1556 the Mughals under the young Akbar and his guardian Bairam Khan defeated Hemchandra Vikramaditya, known as Hemu, at Panipat, after he had taken Delhi and Agra; Hemu was captured and beheaded.

facts.place: Panipat, north of Delhi in present-day India, not far from the site of the First Battle of Panipat of 1526
facts.sides: The Mughals under the 13-year-old Akbar and his guardian Bairam Khan, with the field army led by Ali Quli Khan Shaibani; Hemchandra (Hemu) and his Afghan army, numerically superior, with a 30,000-strong cavalry force and an elephant contingent numbering 500, and no artillery
facts.outcome: Hemu was wounded by an arrow and fell unconscious, and his army broke and fled. The Mughals won, and Hemu was captured and beheaded.

t: Hemu, the Chief Minister and general of the Suri ruler Adil Shah, took Delhi on 7 October 1556 and claimed royal status as Vikramaditya, about a month before the battle.
His army was the larger one, with 500 armoured war elephants, but a Mughal detachment had captured his artillery on the way, and he fought without guns.
The battle was fought as Hemu seemed close to victory: a chance arrow struck him in the eye, he collapsed unconscious, and his army panicked.
dyk: Hemu had been victorious in 22 battles from Bengal to Punjab before Panipat, and the Mughals took 120 of his war elephants, whose rampages impressed them so much that elephants soon became an integral part of Mughal military strategy.
ev: Sher Shah Suri drives Humayun out of India and establishes the Sur Empire
The Mughals defeat Sikandar Shah Suri and regain Delhi and Agra
Humayun dies, and Hemchandra marches from Bengal against the territories the Mughals held
Hemchandra defeats the Mughal governor Tardi Beg Khan and takes Delhi, claiming royal status as Vikramaditya
Ali Quli Khan Shaibani captures Hemchandra's artillery on the march towards Delhi
The Mughals defeat Hemchandra's army at Panipat after he is struck by an arrow
Hemchandra is captured and beheaded, and his head and body are displayed
Adil Shah is defeated and killed by Khizr Khan, son of Muhammad Khan Sur of Bengal

sections.background:
Humayun, the successor of Babur, the founder of the Mughal Empire, lost his inheritance when Sher Shah Suri chased him out of India and established the Sur Empire in 1540. Delhi and Agra fell into Sher Shah's hands, but he died in 1545 at Kalinjar. His younger son, Islam Shah Suri, was a capable ruler, but on his death in 1554 the Sur Empire was caught up in a succession battle and plagued by rebellion and the secession of provinces. Humayun used the discord to recapture what he had lost, and on 23 July 1555 the Mughals defeated Sikandar Shah Suri and regained control of Delhi and Agra.

Islam Shah's rightful successor, his 12-year-old son Firoz Khan, was murdered by his maternal uncle, who took the throne as Adil Shah Suri. The new ruler was more interested in pleasure than in the affairs of state, which were left mainly to Hemchandra, an old Hindu associate of Sher Shah Suri from Rewari. Hemchandra had risen from humble circumstances to become Adil Shah's Chief Minister and the general of the Suri army. He was in Bengal when Humayun died on 27 January 1556, an opportunity to defeat the Mughals and reclaim lost territory.

Hemchandra marched rapidly from Bengal and drove the Mughals out of Bayana, Etawah, Bharthana, Bidhuna, Lakhna, Sambhal, Kalpi and Narnaul. The governor of Agra evacuated the city and fled without a fight. Hemchandra pursued him to Tughlaqabad, a village just outside Delhi, where he met and defeated the forces of the Mughal governor of Delhi, Tardi Beg Khan. He took possession of Delhi after a day's battle on 7 October 1556 and assumed the title of Vikramaditya.
sections.forces:
The Mughal army was led by Ali Quli Khan Shaibani, later Khan-i-Zaman, with his 10,000 cavalry in the centre. Sikandar Khan Uzbak held the right and Abdulla Khan Uzbak the left. The vanguard was led by Husain Quli Beg and Shah Quli Mahram and included Bairam Khan's detachment of Turks. The 13-year-old Akbar, who had succeeded Humayun, and his guardian Bairam Khan did not take part in the fighting: they stayed in the rear, eight miles from the battleground.

Hemu's army was numerically superior. It included a 30,000-strong cavalry force of Afghan horse riders and an elephant contingent numbering 500, each war elephant protected by plate armour and mounted by musketeers and crossbowmen. Hemchandra led his army himself, mounted on an elephant named Hawai. His left was led by his sister's son, Ramya, and the right by Shadi Khan Kakar. The army was experienced and confident, and Hemu had by then been victorious in 22 battles from Bengal to Punjab.

In this battle, however, Hemchandra had no artillery. On the march Ali Quli Khan, who had been sent ahead with a 10,000-strong cavalry force, came upon Hemchandra's artillery being transported under a weak guard. The Afghans abandoned the guns and fled without making a stand, and the Mughals captured the entire train. The loss proved costly for Hemu.
sections.course:
On 5 November 1556 the Mughal army met Hemu's army on the historic battlefield of Panipat. Hemchandra began the attack himself and loosed his elephants against the right and left wings of the Mughals. The soldiers who escaped the rampage did not retreat but veered to the sides and attacked the flanks of Hemu's cavalry, pelting them with their superior archery. The Mughal centre advanced and took up a defensive position before a deep ravine, which neither Hemchandra's elephants nor his horse could cross, leaving them vulnerable to the missiles fired from the other side.

Meanwhile the Mughal cavalry, on swift mounts, made inroads into the Afghan ranks from the flanks and the rear and began targeting the elephants, slashing at their legs or taking out their riders. Hemchandra pulled back his elephants and the Afghan attack relented. Seeing this, Ali Quli Khan led his cavalry out, circled round and fell on the Afghan centre from the rear. Hemu, watching from his howdah atop Hawai, hurried to counter the charge.

Even after Shadi Khan Kakar and another of his lieutenants, Bhagwan Das, went down, Hemu kept leading counterattacks, running down any who challenged his elephants. The battle was desperately contested but the advantage seemed to have tilted towards him. Both Mughal wings had been driven back, and he moved his elephants and cavalry forward to crush their centre. At this point, possibly on the cusp of victory, he was struck in the eye by a chance Mughal arrow and collapsed unconscious. His army, seeing him go down, panicked, broke formation and fled.
sections.aftermath:
The battle was lost. Some 5,000 dead lay on the field, and many more were killed while fleeing. The elephant carrying the unconscious and almost dead Hemchandra was captured several hours after the fighting ended and led to the Mughal camp. Bairam Khan asked the 13-year-old Akbar to behead him. Akbar is said by one account to have refused to take the sword to a dead man, while another says he followed Bairam Khan's advice and beheaded Hemchandra himself and took the title of Ghazi.

Hemchandra's head was sent to Kabul, to be hung outside the Delhi Darwaja, while his body was gibbeted on a gate of the Purana Quila in Delhi, where he had held his coronation on 6 October. Several of his supporters and relatives were also beheaded.

With Hemchandra gone, Adil Shah's fortunes took a turn for the worse. He was defeated and killed by Khizr Khan, son of Muhammad Khan Sur of Bengal, in April 1557. The spoils of Panipat included 120 of Hemu's war elephants.
sections.sources:
Two writers of Akbar's court give the accounts of what became of Hemchandra. Abu'l-Fazl ibn Mubarak, Akbar's later courtier, writes that Akbar refused to take his sword to a dead man. Muhammad Arif Qandhari, a contemporary who composed the Tarikh e Akbari, writes that Akbar followed Bairam Khan's advice and beheaded Hemchandra himself and took the title of Ghazi. The account of Akbar's refusal is probably a later invention of his courtiers.

The Akbarnama is also a source of images: a painting of the minaret raised after the battle is one of the 56 paintings of Akbar's life in the Akbarnama copy. Both writers served or wrote under the Mughal court, so the fate of Hemu is known from the victors' side.
sections.legacy:
Hemu's march from Bengal had briefly put Delhi and Agra in his hands, and the battle was fought to take them back. The Mughals, who had regained the two cities in July 1555, held them after Panipat, and Adil Shah was himself defeated and killed within months.

The captured elephants left a mark on Mughal warfare. Their destructive rampages so impressed the Mughals that elephants soon became an integral part of Mughal military strategy. Hemu is also commemorated at Panipat: a memorial was erected at the spot where he was beheaded, and it is now known as Hemu's Samadhi Sthal.

Akbar, 13 years old at the time of the battle and kept eight miles from the fighting, is said to have taken the title of Ghazi after it. The battle was fought not far from the site of the First Battle of Panipat of 1526.

summary: On 5 November 1556 the Mughal army of the young Akbar and Bairam Khan defeated Hemchandra Vikramaditya at Panipat, a month after he had taken Delhi. A chance arrow struck Hemu down as he seemed close to winning, his army fled, and he was captured and beheaded.
notes: The article names Hemu's earlier fight both 'Battle of Delhi' (lead) and 'Battle of Tughlaqabad' (background); I told it as a fight at Tughlaqabad that gave him Delhi on 7 October 1556.

The article says Hemu took Delhi on 7 October but also that he was crowned at the Purana Quila on 6 October (aftermath), and the lead gives 'a few weeks earlier'. I kept both dates as written; the order is odd.

Left out as garbled: 'a minaret was later erected', which the article does not connect clearly to the battle's dead; in sources I mention only that the Akbarnama painting of the minaret is one of its 56 paintings.
The article says Hemu's head was 'sent to Kabul to be hanged outside Delhi Darwaja': kept as written, but Kabul and a Delhi gate do not sit easily together.
No Mughal total strength is given. The 5,000 dead is the only casualty figure and is not attributed. The article does not say which side's dead.
The article contradicts itself on whether Akbar beheaded Hemu: lead and Qandhari say yes, Abu'l-Fazl no. Both given. The lead also says 'Hemu was captured and subsequently beheaded by Akbar'.
The sources section is thin: the article names only Abu'l-Fazl, Qandhari and the Akbarnama painting. A four-line verse is quoted without attribution and omitted.

'Legacy' is thin in the article; the section rests on the elephants, the memorial, and Adil Shah's fall. The sentence on the end of the Afghan attempt is the writer's summary from the article's narrative and should be read by the editor.
